ta-l1d40q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 40. Having treated God's knowledge in general, Lombard treats predestination: what it is, and then (Dist. 41) its causality, whether it is a first cause or has another cause. On the first he treats predestination, what it is and of whom, and its certainty (none of the predestined can be damned), with an objection, a response, a renewed objection, and a solution he would rather hear from others; then reprobation, the foreknowledge of some people's iniquity, as the converse of predestination, the preparation of grace. Thomas asks two questions, on predestination and on reprobation. On predestination, three topics: what it is, of whom, and its certainty; on the first, whether predestination is in the creature or only in God, and what it names in God.
claims: Predestination is the preparation of grace; reprobation the foreknowledge of iniquity.
None of the predestined can be damned.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e131.summary: First argument that predestination is something in the predestined. Every action implies a passion, and 'God predestines' signifies a divine act, so there is a passion in the creature, passive predestination, as with creation, which is both action and passion.
claims: Every action has a corresponding passion.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e134.summary: Second argument. Every denomination is by an inherent form, and something is called predestined by predestination.
claims: Denomination requires inherence.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e137.summary: Third argument. Comparison is between things of one genus, and the Gloss on John 1 says it was better for Nathanael to know the two natures in Christ than to be predestined, and that knowledge posits something in him.
claims: Predestination is compared with knowledge in Nathanael.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e144.summary: Fourth argument. Nothing eternal is defined by the temporal, but predestination is defined as the preparation of grace in the present and glory in the future, so it is not eternal, and every action said of God temporally posits an effect in the creature, like ruling.
claims: Predestination is defined by temporal effects.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e147.summary: Sed contra. Only the predestined are elected, and those who do not exist are elected (Augustine), so predestination is of non-beings, in which nothing can be.
claims: Non-existents are elected.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e150.summary: Second sed contra. Predestination is a species of divine knowledge (Dist. 38), and knowledge is nothing in the known, only in the knower.
claims: Knowledge is in the knower.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e153.summary: Thomas's determination. Positing something in another is understood two ways: as the thing signified by the name being in it, as whiteness posits something in the white, and so predestination posits nothing in the predestined, only in the predestiner; or as something following in the other from what is signified in one, as paternity, though only in the father, posits something in the son. The latter happens either simultaneously, as paternity leaves filiation, or not necessarily simultaneously, before or after, as hearing posits a sounding stroke simultaneous or prior. In this way predestination posits something in the predestined, since from this divine operation the effect of predestination follows in the predestined, not whenever predestination is but at some time, and this effect is grace and glory.
claims: Predestination is in God alone, but its effect, grace and glory, follows in the predestined in time.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e156.summary: Reply to the first argument. Some actions pass into external matter producing an effect, natural (fire heating wood) or artificial (building a house), and there the action is received in what is made as passion, as motion is in the moved, so there is action in the agent and passion in the patient. Others, like vision, produce no effect in the thing seen and are properly called operations, existing only in the operator, so the passion corresponds to the external thing not as it is in itself but only as it is in the operator, as the stone is seen only as in the eye by its likeness. Creation leaves an external effect, so passive creation is something in the creature, as heating in the heated; predestination names an operation of will and intellect existing only in the operator, like vision or speculation, so taken passively it is nothing in the predestined as considered in itself, but only as in the predestiner by the likeness by which it is known, and the predestined is named so by the predestiner's operation, as a thing is called seen by the seer's. Alternatively: some operation is signified as passing into an effect, properly action or passion, with a corresponding passion (heating, creation); other operation is signified as something in the agent, and if received, the reception is passion and the act following the composite of received and receiver is operation, since operation belongs to the perfect, as sensing, which as reception of the species is passion, as is understanding (De anima 3), and as act following the sense perfected by the species is operation, the act of the perfect. In God the likeness of the known is by his essence, not by reception, so his understanding implies no passion, only operation. Such operations have corresponding passions only in mode of signifying, as being known posits no real passion in the known, only a conceptual respect to the knower, signified by grammarians as passive. So predestination is a divine operation, and being predestined posits no passion in the predestined, only a respect in our mode of understanding, left by the assimilation of the known in the knower.
claims: Predestination is an immanent operation, not a transitive action, so it posits no passion in the predestined.
Unlike creation, which leaves an external effect, predestination is like vision.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the second argument. In absolute things something is denominated by what is in it, but in relatives sometimes by what is in it (father by paternity) and sometimes by what is only in another, where the relation is real in one and conceptual in the other, as the knowable is called relative not because it is referred but because another is referred to it (the Philosopher). So predestination is really nothing except in the divine intellect.
claims: The predestined is denominated by a relation real only in God.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e163.summary: Reply to the third argument. The comparison is not of knowing the two natures absolutely with predestination, but of knowledge together with predestination with predestination together with the Old Law's state, since predestination holds with both: it is better to be predestined with the grace of the New Testament than predestined without it, since predestination runs through both testaments.
claims: The comparison is of predestination with and without New Testament grace.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e169.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The temporal is not placed in the definition of the eternal directly, as denoting its substance, but nothing prevents placing it obliquely, to signify the eternal's relation to the temporal, and so grace and glory are placed in the definition of predestination.
claims: Grace and glory enter the definition obliquely.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e181.summary: First argument that predestination belongs to knowledge. The text says predestination cannot be without foreknowledge, which names knowledge with an order to the future.
claims: Predestination requires foreknowledge.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e184.summary: Second argument that it belongs to will. Augustine says predestination is the purpose of having mercy, and purposing is an act of will, determining an end.
claims: Predestination is a purpose.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e187.summary: Third argument that it belongs to power. Preparing is an act of power, and predestination is the preparation of God's benefits.
claims: Predestination prepares.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e191.summary: Fourth argument that it is the same as providence or disposition, since predestination is the direction of something to an end, which belongs to providence.
claims: Predestination directs to an end.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e194.summary: Fifth argument that it is the same as the book of life. The soul's life is by grace and glory, and predestination is the preparation of grace in the present and glory in the future.
claims: Predestination concerns the life of grace and glory.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e197.summary: Thomas's determination. Predestination includes providence and adds at least three things. On the side of the predestined: providence is of all, and specially of those with will, and predestination includes providence in that special mode, of humans and those with will. On the side of the end and what promotes it: providence regards the order of every good to any end, predestination only what is raised above natural capacity, glory, perfect enjoyment of God, and grace promoting it, so Damascene says predestination is of what is not in us. On the side of the predestiner, two things: providence is the art of governing things, which by its name can hold in speculation alone, but predestination implies providence as ordered to execution by will, so it is defined by purpose and preparation; and it adds foreknowledge of the outcome, since something can depart from the order of providence as to what is intended (God wills all to be saved, though not all are), but not from the order of predestination, which says God's intention of this person's salvation with foreknowledge that he will be saved, so it is called foreknowledge and preparation.
claims: Predestination is a special providence over rational creatures, ordered to supernatural ends, with purpose of will and foreknowledge of the outcome.
Something can escape the intention of providence but not the order of predestination.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e200.summary: This answers the first argument: more than foreknowledge is placed in its definition.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the second argument. 'Purpose' does not simply name an act of will but presupposes an act of cognition showing the end the will tends to.
claims: Purpose presupposes cognition.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the third argument. The preparation in the definition of predestination is not by execution in the work but is understood by the purpose of the divine will.
claims: Preparation here means purpose, not execution.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e210.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Predestination is a mode of providence but adds special features to it.
claims: Predestination is a special providence.

ta-l1d40q1-d1e213.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. 'Book of life' is said metaphorically: as something is written in a book from which its truth is understood, likenesses of things are inscribed in the intellect, by which they are known, so the possible intellect is a blank tablet (De anima 3). 'Life' in the book of life can be taken on the side of God understanding, so foreknowledge of creatures is the book of life, since what was made was life in him (John 1:3), or on the side of the thing known, so the book of life is the foreknowledge of the life that consists in conformity to God, of grace and of glory, which approaches perfect conformity. Someone whose life of glory is represented in the book of divine foreknowledge is written in the book of life simply; someone whose life of grace only, as to present justice, in some respect; and in a way their opposites are written there too, as known through them. So the book of life is midway between foreknowledge in general, of all things, and predestination: it is knowledge of grace or glory only, while predestination is of grace and glory together. So no one is called predestined as to present justice, as one is called written in the book of life, and predestination adds the purpose of will.
claims: The book of life is God's foreknowledge of the life of grace or glory, midway between foreknowledge and predestination.
concepts: written simply vs. in some respect

ta-l1d40q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 40 divides Lombard's treatment of predestination (what it is, of whom, its certainty) and reprobation, and announces two questions, the first with articles on whether predestination is in the creature and what it names in God.
claims: Predestination is the preparation of grace.

ta-l1d40q1-Dd1e123.summary: Article 1 holds that predestination is in God alone, an immanent operation of intellect and will like vision, positing no passion in the predestined, though its effect, grace and glory, follows in time. The predestined is denominated by a relation real only in God, the Gloss compares predestination with and without New Testament grace, and grace and glory enter its definition obliquely.
claims: Predestination is in God; its effect is grace and glory in the predestined.

ta-l1d40q1-Dd1e173.summary: Article 2 holds that predestination is a special providence over rational creatures, ordered to the supernatural ends of grace and glory, with purpose of will and foreknowledge of the outcome, so that nothing escapes its order as things can escape the intention of providence. The book of life is midway between foreknowledge and predestination, knowledge of the life of grace or glory.
claims: Predestination adds to providence: rational subjects, supernatural end, purpose, and certain outcome.

ta-l1d40q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 40 treats what predestination is. Article 1 holds that it is an immanent operation in God, positing nothing in the predestined except its temporal effect, grace and glory. Article 2 holds that it is a special mode of providence over rational creatures, directed to grace and glory, including purpose of will and foreknowledge of the outcome, and distinguishes it from the book of life.
claims: Predestination is in God and its effect is grace and glory.
Predestination is a special providence with purpose and certain foreknowledge.
